name: The Anchoring Effect
brief: Whoever names a price first sets the tone (car haggling, salary negotiation)
fail: Against a pro buyer holding a firm competing quote, the anchor barely grips — the first-move advantage nearly vanishes.

name: How Extreme an Anchor Can Go
brief: When to dare a bold ask — and when it blows up the deal
fail: When they have endless alternatives and walking away costs them nothing, an extreme ask kills the deal before bargaining even starts.

name: Precise Numbers Anchor Harder
brief: The more precise the quote, the harder to haggle down (€14,875 holds firmer than €15,000)
fail: Once they see through the "precision implies homework" trick and demand an item-by-item breakdown, the precise anchor collapses.

name: The Reciprocity Rule
brief: Every concession must buy something back
fail: When they read your concession as a calculated ploy rather than goodwill, it buys nothing — and reads as weakness.

name: Whoever's More Desperate Loses
brief: The side with the costlier clock concedes first
fail: When they genuinely don't care whether the deal happens, you can't win a waiting game — change the chips instead.

name: The Repeated Game
brief: Never play ruthless with people you'll meet again (regulars, long-term suppliers)
fail: Against a stranger who vanishes after one deal, cooperation is charity — play the hard one-shot game.

name: Loss Aversion
brief: People fear losing more than they crave gaining (insurance pitches, promo copy decoded)
fail: When the loss is too small to feel — pocket change — or they've gone fully numb to it, the loss frame moves no one.

name: Reference Points
brief: Same fact, different wording, different outcome — includes: spotting their reference point fast
fail: When they catch you playing framing games and bristle, rewording only deepens the distrust.

name: The Desperate Gambler
brief: Someone deep in the red dares bigger bets (the reflection effect — why loss-framing backfires on them)
fail: If they still see one concrete path to recovery, loss-framing pushes them toward even bigger risks — first confirm they're truly out of options.

name: When Gain-Framing Wins
brief: Tell someone in a hole what they can still save
fail: When they're riding high and risk-averse, gain-framing makes them more conservative — use the loss frame to move them.

name: Turn It on Yourself
brief: Write your goals as "what I'll lose by not acting"
fail: When the goal is so big the "loss" is unimaginable (like health), loss-writing only manufactures anxiety — shrink the goal first.

name: The Zero-Base Question
brief: "If I'd just inherited this project today, would I still fund it?"
fail: When the project carries irreversible reputational lock-in (a public promise), the honest answer warps — the exit cost isn't on the books, it's on your face.

name: Option Value
brief: When to keep it alive instead of killing it (quitting vs. keeping the pilot light on)
fail: When keeping it alive costs more than the option itself is worth, "keeping the pilot light" is procrastination — kill it.

name: Pre-Commitment
brief: Write the rules before you start
fail: When the world changes so the rules' premises no longer hold, clinging to old rules is navigating today with yesterday's map.

name: Sunk Cost
brief: For a trapped position, ask not "will it recover?" but "would I buy it today?"
fail: When the position carries an unreplicable information edge or tax/structural reasons, "would I buy today" can't directly dictate selling.

name: Sunk Costs in Careers & Relationships
brief: Five years of experience vs. five years of shackles
fail: When those five years converted into portable assets (method, network), they're not shackles — tuition already paid.

name: Escalation of Commitment
brief: The more you pour in, the harder it is to stop
fail: When new money genuinely changes the odds (a breakthrough actually near) rather than "one more bet," escalation doesn't apply — staying in is arithmetic.

name: The 2-Minute Start
brief: Just write the title, 120 seconds (dreaded tasks: expenses, data cleanup, routine reports — start first)
fail: When the task's direction is wrong (strategy chaos), starting fast just walks you efficiently in the wrong direction — stop and decompose first.

name: Habit Stacking
brief: Weld the new move onto an old habit
fail: When the old habit itself is unstable (travel, broken sleep), the welded-on move breaks with it — fix the anchor first.

name: Environment Design
brief: Make starting easy, make distraction hard
fail: When distraction comes from the task being meaningless rather than tempting surroundings, rearranging the room is useless — first answer "is this worth doing."

name: Why Bedtime Thinking Keeps You Awake
brief: The default-mode network idling at full speed
fail: When the anxiety hides one unexamined key risk, physical interruption is avoidance — write the risk down first.

name: Attention Restoration
brief: Change the scenery to recharge (walks and nature work best)
fail: When fatigue comes from decision exhaustion rather than monotony, walks recharge little — cut the decision load first.

name: Rumination vs. Review
brief: One spins its wheels, the other moves forward
fail: When it's not over and information is incomplete, forced "review" becomes convicting yourself on partial evidence — gather first.

name: Exercise as Circuit-Breaker
brief: Why your head clears after a run
fail: When the body is already overdrawn or injured, exercise deepens the deficit — sleep or stillness instead.

name: Consensus Is Priced In
brief: An "opportunity" everyone knows about has no profit left by the time it reaches you
fail: Early, before the information has spread and consensus has formed, "priced in" doesn't apply yet.

name: The Mediocrity of Being Balanced
brief: Why AI's "balanced view" can't guide action (an inference from RLHF mechanics)
source: Christiano et al. 2017；Ouyang et al. 2022（推论）
fail: When the task only needs average (sorting info, running process), the balanced view is the efficient choice — don't burn compute hunting anti-consensus.

name: The Arms-Race Equilibrium
brief: When everyone uses the same tool, the edge goes to zero (everyone writes résumés with AI; HR sees through all of them)
fail: When how you use the tool has a know-how moat (prompt craft, domain experience), everyone having it does not equal everyone wielding it equally.

name: The Beauty Contest
brief: Everyone's guessing not the truth but what others think
fail: When every player is a fundamentals-driven long-term investor, the guessing-game layers don't apply — look at value itself.

name: Information Cascades
brief: Rational individuals ditch private info to follow the crowd (the longest queue isn't the tastiest)
fail: When predecessors' actions carry verifiable hard info (published financials) rather than pure following, following is rational information use, not herd blindness.

name: Kill Your Own Consensus
brief: Falsificationism — hand-kill one deeply held judgment every week
fail: When the judgment itself is unfalsifiable ("tomorrow it goes up, down, or sideways" covers everything), forced falsification wastes a week — first check the proposition is well-formed.

name: Positional Competition
brief: The neighbors' kid has it, so mine can't go without — you're not buying the thing, you're buying the ranking
fail: When comparison carries real information (everyone buys because it's good), that's an information cascade. When the game itself is ranking (sports, exams), competition isn't the trap — the mistake is running a status race as if it were a value race.

name: Working Memory Limits
brief: You can juggle about 4 things in your head (7 to-dos in one meeting guarantees drops)
fail: Once information is chunked (a veteran hears one long number as a single unit), the 4-chunk cap doesn't bind — it limits chunks, not information.

name: Attention Residue
brief: The last task's thoughts follow you into the next one (after a heated meeting, every proposal looks wrong)
fail: With a clear closing ritual between tasks (write the conclusion, shut the notebook), residue drops sharply — residue fears "unfinished," not "switching."

name: The Retrieval Practice Effect
brief: Before an exam, close the book and recite once — beats re-reading three times
fail: When the knowledge never got in (you didn't understand it the first pass), forced recitation is carving on blank stone — understand first, retrieve second.

name: The Peak-End Rule
brief: People remember an experience by its peak and its ending (colonoscopy: long pain with a gentle ending gets rated "not that bad")
fail: When the rating comes from tallying a complete record (scoring against the full bill) rather than memory, peak-end doesn't apply — it governs "the remembered feeling," not "the computed total."

name: Regression to the Mean
brief: This year's top scorer likely slips next year — not arrogance, just luck fading
fail: Doesn't apply across structural breaks (new coach, new rules, paradigm shifts) — the mean itself is drifting.

name: Base-Rate Neglect
brief: Hearing "tested positive" and panicking, without asking how rare the condition is
fail: When the base rate itself is unknown or shifting fast (early days of a new virus), "check the base rate first" has nothing to stand on — admit ignorance first.

name: Survivorship Bias
brief: We only hear success stories, because failures never get book deals
fail: When failed samples are available and included in the analysis, the bias is corrected — "beware survivorship bias" is not a universal shield.

name: The Law of Large Numbers
brief: 7 heads in 10 flips is normal; 10,000 flips lands near half
fail: When trials aren't independent (contagion, herding, feedback loops), the premise collapses — ask "independent?" before talking convergence.

name: Vividness Effect
brief: The mind is moved by a vivid single case and numb to abstract numbers
fail: When the case agrees with the base rate, trusting it is fine — the error is trusting only it. Flip it around: turn dry statistics into a vivid story, and vividness becomes a tool, not a trap.

name: The Michelson–Morley Experiment
brief: A "failed" experiment that killed the aether
fail: If "detecting nothing" came from instruments too crude to detect anything, a null result is not falsification — check precision before declaring death.

name: The Death of Phlogiston
brief: Lavoisier weighed "phlogiston" out of existence
fail: Until the new theory's predictions become measurable numbers, don't rush to declare the old theory dead — build the scale first.

name: The Ulcer Bacteria Bet
brief: Two doctors drank the bacteria to prove ulcers aren't "just stress"
fail: When a self-experiment can't rule out placebo and individual variation, the conclusion is only "worth large-scale testing," not "proven" — drinking the bacteria is the starting line, not the finish.

name: The Dichotomy of Control
brief: Sort your worries into two piles — what I can move, what I can't
fail: Fails when "only control the controllable" becomes an excuse to dodge necessary action ("the market's uncontrollable, so why review") — the first controllable item is the act of reviewing itself.

name: Premeditatio Malorum
brief: Spend a minute a day on "how bad could it get" — when it comes, you won't panic
fail: Fails when rehearsal becomes looping the worst case on repeat, manufacturing chronic anxiety — rehearse once, write the plan, then stop. No reruns.

name: Amor Fati (Only for What's Done)
brief: Money already lost: call it tuition, not fate
source: Marcus Aurelius《沉思录》约180（"amor fati"一词 Nietzsche 1882）
fail: Fails on what hasn't happened and can still change — resigning to the future is giving up; amor fati governs only the past.

name: Win First, Then Fight
brief: Before engaging, decide in advance where you'll admit defeat
source: 《孙子兵法·形篇》约公元前5世纪
fail: Fails when "waiting for better odds" becomes never opening a position — waiting itself turns into an excuse for inaction; winning-first is preparation, not delay.

name: Prize Victory, Not Duration
brief: A battle you can't win only compounds losses the longer you drag it
source: 《孙子兵法·作战篇》约公元前5世纪
fail: When dragging is accumulating advantage (waiting on earnings, on technical confirmation) and the cost is contained, "strike fast" is the wrong call — price the delay before calling the stop.

name: Know Where to Stop
brief: Before entering, decide: where you walk away in profit, where you walk away in loss
fail: When structural change voids the original exit terms — with a written revision on record — you may revise; the revision itself must name a new line in the sand. No verbal edits.

name: Wu Wei
brief: Don't predict; only respond
fail: When the variables are actually controllable and predictable (your own position, your own discipline), "wu wei" becomes an excuse for laziness — non-action applies only to the uncontrollable.
